title: The Birth of Photography
subject: art
description: In **1839**, several inventors finally worked out how to fix an image on a plate. In less than a century, photography changed the way we see, remember, and believe.

hero.hook: How a chemical invention stole painting's monopoly on the real.

blocks.text: For centuries, artists used the [[camera obscura]], a dark box that throws the outside world onto a wall. The problem never changed: the image vanishes the moment the light goes out. In **1839**, photography was officially born. It was not the work of one genius, but a race between French and British inventors.
In less than a century, the process freed painting from its role as a document and became the first mass medium. It changed our relationship to time, to memory, and to visual truth.

It all started with **Nicéphore Niépce**, a French inventor. Around **1826-1827**, he fixed the first permanent image, *View from the Window*. He coated a pewter plate with [[bitumen of Judea]], a tar that hardens in light. The exposure lasted about **8 hours**, long enough for the sun to light both sides of the buildings.

blocks.caption: The oldest known photograph, taken by Niépce from his window

blocks.text: In that image, the shadows on both facades are visible at the same time: the exposure ran so long that the sun crossed the whole sky.

After Niépce died, his partner **Louis Daguerre** discovered what iodine and mercury vapor do to silver. He perfected the **daguerreotype**, presented to the Academy of Sciences in **1839**. In England, at the same time, [[William Fox Talbot's calotype]] appeared, a paper process that could print several copies from a single negative.

sections.title: A portrait for everyone, proof for everyone

blocks.text: From the **1840s**, photography left the laboratory. Until then, having your portrait made was a luxury for anyone who could pay a painter. With the studios and the [[carte-de-visite]], a small and cheap format, the middle classes and then working people gained an image of themselves.

blocks.caption: The daguerreotype: a single image of startling detail, on a silver plate

blocks.text: Photography also became proof. During the Crimean War (**1855**), **Roger Fenton** brought back pictures from the front. During the American Civil War, **Mathew Brady** photographed the soldiers and the battlefields. An event was no longer only told. It was shown.

sections.title: When painting had to reinvent itself

blocks.text: If a machine copies a face better than a painter can, what is painting still for? Here lies the [[impact of photography on figurative painting]]: figurative art lost its monopoly on the real. Freed from that duty, artists went looking elsewhere, first for the sensation of light with [[Impressionism]], then for the breaking of form with [[Cubism]].
Photography, for its part, slowly claimed a language of its own: framing, light, the instant. It was no longer a plain copy of the world. It became an art in full.

sections.title: Kodak and the culture of the image

blocks.text: At the end of the 19th century, **George Eastman**, the founder of Kodak, replaced heavy glass plates with flexible film. The camera became portable. The slogan “You press the button, we do the rest” marked the birth of the amateur. The family album and the global news report were born together.

blocks.text: Born in **1839**, photography first captured the real better than painting could, then invented our modern [[visual culture]], the one where we believe what we see first.
